paragraphs.text: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = “with”) the trends of life… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, “that which co-exists with hita [welfare]”. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, “Art for artʼs sake,” cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement “Art for artʼs sake” is not acceptable; rather we should say, “Art for service and blessedness.”… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

paragraphs.text: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“The Practice of Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted from above. But he did not stop there. Advancing further, he translated his words into actions, creating a direct example in the form of his own literature, marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus we get a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part set was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that we are extremely happy to present to the readers now Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

paragraphs.text: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of linguistics and philology which touched also on history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books. Apart from the books mentioned above, some stories are from a volume of the authorʼs childrenʼs literature series – namely, In the Land of Hat́t́amálá.

paragraphs.text: Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs discourses, as published, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise wording the author used in speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words. As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. ‘Man is mortal’ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

paragraphs.text: The people of Ráŕh [land of laterite soil; a territory mostly in West Bengal, stretching from the west bank of Bhagirathi River to the Parasnath Hills] engage in serious philosophical exercises as much as they engage in light-hearted play; they are full of life – with laughter, amusements, dance, song, wit and humour (rága and rauṋga). They are sociable and prefer to remain in each otherʼs company and in a cheerful mood (khos mejájii) in a gathering. Though burdened with poverty, they invite people for meals. They serve what they themselves eat – rice, black gram (biŕi in Ráŕhii Bengali), baŕi-posta [dumplings made of pulse, flavoured with poppy seeds], curry and pumpkin (d́iḿlá in Ráŕhii Bengali). They are not inhibited in their behaviour due to their poverty. They are not shy to say clearly what ought to be said. Here is an example of the straightforwardness of the people of Ráŕh: ( 1 )

The latter, in a letter to his Kolkata office from Tatanagar, had used two “t”s in the word “benefit”. When the letter reached Mr. S.P. Banerjee, he called the other Banerjee and said, “My dear Gour, why did you double the ”t“?”

paragraphs.text: The mother explained, “A woman who does not have a son has just one regret. She goes around lamenting that she is childless. A woman whose son has died also has just one regret. She beats her head in sorrow and cries, 'Oh, my son is gone forever, no one will call me má anymore!ʼ But a mother whose son is a fool is doomed forever. On the one hand, she is in misery all the time and on the other, her neighbours call upon her day in and day out to complain about the foolish deeds committed by the son. Listening and listening to all these noises day in and day out I am extremely vexed; my heart is keen to flee. Hence learned men have said, it is better not to have a son at all or even lose a son to death, rather than be saddled with a fool of a son all your life. If such is the case, a mother has to endure agony every moment. You can very well see the plight I am in with this fool Dantavikásh [literal meaning is to display oneʼs teeth foolishly]. Even the fox in the wild and mosquitoes in watery bogs cry in sympathy. Just see with your own eyes how cruelly he beat me on my back. It is swollen like a guŕ-pit́he.”

footnotes.text: God is known as shliipada in Sanskrit, elephantiasis in English and phiilpáo in Urdu. Phil in Persian is hátii (elephant). In olden days, the place where kings stabled their elephants was called hátiishálá in Bengali and philkháná in Persian. In colloquial Bengali, this word was mispronounced as pilkháná. You can still find some pilkhánáʼs in the old city. In chess, the elephant is also called phil.

Many varieties of betel leaves like báuṋglá pán, tolá pán, mit́he pán, cháṋci pán, magahii pán are produced in Bengal. It was an old custom here for the bride to keep her face covered with one – the stalk upwards and the pointed end downwards – during a marriage ceremony. Báuṋglá pán was used for this purpose because of its large size. There were innumerable rites (ácára) and rituals practiced in the olden days during such a ceremony.

In olden times, different customary rites like deshácár, striiácár, lokácár, kulácár were performed during the marriage ceremony. These rites [ácár] are in no way associated with the acár [pickles] of kula [berry].

paragraphs.text: Shráddhe ca bhuribhojanam was a custom in the past. This meant that the invitees to a shráddha [a feast held after funeral rites are performed] were to be treated in a grand fashion. In its common usage, the meaning of the word bhuri is “plenty”, and in this context the quantity of luci, sweets, etc. that was packed inside the guestʼs stomach was to be served on an adjacent plate in an equal amount. After the meal was over, the other plateful of food was tied up in a bundle (cháṋdá) and taken home by the guest. Even after a surfeit of food (such a huge meal had been taken that the food had risen past the abdomen and chest and reached the throat), it was only when the guest carried an equal amount home that it was accepted that it had indeed been a grand feast (bhuribhojana).

paragraphs.text: The use of cha is prevalent in the native dialects of Bengal but it is pronounced differently in various dialects. The cha sound in a foreign word is pronounced as cha or ca or even as sa in the Bengali dialects of different regions. Many use the letter cha to represent the sa sound in Arabic words. Although it does not correctly represent the Arabic sa sound, there is nothing wrong with it because it tries to emulate a distinctive pronunciation at least. Therefore, there is no problem in using both forms of spellings for words like Syed and Chyed, Islam and Echlam, Basiruddin and Bachiruddin.

paragraphs.text: Of all types of hypocritical behaviour, we are more familiar with three very common patterns. The first is to exploit others or deceive them in order to fulfill oneʼs own interests. The second is to browbeat others to hide oneʼs own ignorance or fault, and the third is to castigate an offence publicly with a view to proving oneʼs innocence, when in fact one is actually a party to the crime.

paragraphs.text: The train was very crowded. It was quite obvious from a look at his fellow passengers that they were not going to disembark at Ranaghat or Porada or even Santahar. Mr Nag remained standing. After some time, he suddenly spoke, “Now I understand why Gandhijii advised me never to travel in a crowded compartment. We are small people and so I thought that he was probably worried about my own comfort. But the thought never crossed his mind. Gandhijii is a great man, much more superior to ordinary people like us. He then explained, “I am telling you all of this not for your own convenience. I am feeling sorry about the discomfort of your fellow passengers because as soon as you enter the crowded compartment, the head count goes up by one, causing more inconvenience to them!” I am always overwhelmed with deep respect for the man [Gandhijii] when I think of his wonderful words. I consider myself exceptionally fortunate for having had the opportunity to serve him. I feel honoured, honoured.”

footnotes.text: The original Sanskrit word is byámoh (bi-á-muh + al ). Apparently, ghaiṋ inflection is used, but actually, due to an ungrammatical but considered correct usage by the sages, the inflection al has been used. The words krodha (anger), droha (enmity) and veda (the Vedas) are derived in the same manner. On the basis of the ghaiṋ-alao puḿsi [the word formed with suffix ghaiṋ or alau will always be masculine gender] aphorism, all these words are of masculine gender.

Also, you can get these here by the dozen if you are willing to shell out money. Shiva is very easy to please. He is satisfied with whatever you offer to Him. He will not be unhappy if you give him dhotis made of coarse cloth, but I could not allow that! How can I ask him to wear cheap cloth? I have not lost my senses, have I? The other night, the Mother Goddess came in my dream. She said, 'I know that you work very hard in your profession. You walk miles in the sun and rain to reach the house of your devotees. I know that you were harassed (nástánábud ( 2 ) ) to the extreme on your way to Chandannagore the other day. My heart bled in sorrow for your sake. Tell your devotee to donate to you a cycle of the latest design and a good quality umbrella this time. You are my son. Tell him that I shall be pleased if he gives you a cycle and an umbrella.ʼ She further added, 'Tell your disciple that both are available in the central market in Chandannagore. He does not have to travel all the way to Kolkata to buy, and since he will be going to the central market, let him also buy five seers of sweet (gajá) [a type of sweet made of flour] to be given away as offering. It will look nice.”

footnotes.text: Mahánád, situated in Hooghly district, was an important cultural centre of Bengal during the Buddhist period. For some time, it was also the capital of Ráŕh until it was inundated with sand during a flood. Thereafter, the capital was moved to Pandua (also in Hooghly district). Pandua was later destroyed in the middle of Pathan rule. The minaret (peṋŕor piir) of Pandua was built at that time.

paragraphs.text: He continued, “Potato is a major crop in Dhanekhali area. We did not keep sheep as pets because they dig up and eat the potatoes in the field. There were a number of ponds in our village with young, good quality fish, especially of the rui, kátlá and mrgel (mirik in western Ráŕh) variety. Rudd fish (kálibáus in western Ráŕh) was particularly good. The best district in Ráŕh is Hooghly, of which the best village is Takipur where our pond surrounded by palm trees is the best. Some rui fish in it are huge – as large as twenty buffaloes put together. They are so big... oh, how shall I show you the size! This is the problem... they were truly large... very large... as large as...” So saying, he extended his hands sideways and scooped up some water. “Sooo big... and do you know how wide they are?” As he said that he revolved his hands in a half-circle and sprinkled the water on his bald pate. footnotes.text: Owing to a lack of historical and linguistic perspective, some people spell sura as shúr, which is completely wrong. Actually, sura means a good man. The gods of mythology regarded themselves as good people and their enemies as bad. They called themselves sura and their enemies as asura. Suras were in reality of the Aryan clan. In Madhya Pradesh and Palamau District in Bihar today, there are some tribes of the asura race. I have seen them at Mahuát́áṋŕ in Palamau. In ancient times, the Aryans – who were actually Caucasians – were of fair or earthy complexion, while the [Turks] and asuras (Assyrians) of the Semitic race had dark or coppery skin. In those days, sura and asura could be easily distinguished by the colour of their skin, but not these days. About three thousand years ago, there was extensive racial blending in the Middle East and South Asia.

Dadru in Sanskrit became daddu in Prakrta, which later came to be known as dád in Bengali. It is a skin disease called ringworm in English and dináy in Hindi. D́ávád́ means “a special gift” in [the ancient] Semitic language. D́ád́ in old Hebrew and dád in old Arabic were derived from d́ávád́. However, this is not a skin disease. The names Álidád and Rahimdád are heard occasionally in Central Asia. Dádpur derived its name in a similar manner from Dánpur or Dattapur, that is, [a place] famous for its generosity.
Takipur is a little village in Hooghly district.

I have studied a lot, taught in a college and a school of Sanskrit, and practised a little ayurvedic medicine. In those days I used to manufacture medicine of world-wide repute in my ayurvedic laboratory. There I made 'palatial-house powderʼ (brhat att́áliká curńa) and ‘giant elephant and gold compounded tablets’ (svarńaghatita subrhat hastii bhasma vatiká), and thousands upon thousands of them were sold each month. Now, you see, when success goes to oneʼs head, one loses compassion for oneʼs fellow men. That, indeed, happened to me. I took to adulterating my products. And then, in course of time, I lost everything. Today I am penniless, destitute, the scum of the earth. Dear prince, I have committed many sins and, as a result, have become Ekánoŕe ghost, and have had to set up house in the palm tree. Until these sins are neutralized by virtuous deeds, I wonʼt have peace of mind. Even now I think, twenty-four hours a day I think, in what way I may atone for these sins. Whenever I get the opportunity I try my best to do good to others. Always keep in mind, prince, that a bad deed will never have good results, and a good deed will never have bad results.”

I can clearly remember, prince, that we once had such a severely cold winter that everything was quickly frozen, and even the waters of the river Ganges turned into ice. I wanted to take the launch from Chinsurah fish market to Naihati [24 Parganas District]. However, the launch service had stopped. After all, you canʼt expect a launch to travel over ice. As I wasnʼt one to be easily deterred, I drove over the ice of the Ganges on a motorcycle and in just one minute reached Naihati. There was no need to drive over the ice to get to Howrah from Calcutta as thereʼs a bridge. But a number of times I amused myself by driving up as far as Salkia Bandhaghat [in Howrah District] from Ahiritola [in Kolkata]. Oh, what a thrilling experience. Just thinking about it makes me jump with joy. Oh yes, let me return to what I was talking about. For some days during that very winter I milked the cow. On milking her I was astonished: 'My goodness, what happened to the condensed milk?ʼ It had turned to ice-cream. After that, for fifteen days at a stretch ice-cream came out of the cowʼs udder. summary: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to mov
points.body: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = “with”) the trends of life… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, “that which co-exists with hita [welfare]”. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, “Art for artʼs sake,” cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement “Art for artʼs sake” is not acceptable; rather we should say, “Art for service and blessedness.”… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

points.body: The range and scope of short stories are exactly the same as those of plays, but short-story writers must know the technique of presenting a long story concisely. Suspense is equally effective in short stories as in plays; dramatic skill is essential for the writer of those short stories which come in the category of sketches, because a sketch holds an intermediate position between a story and a play.”

summary: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (
points.body: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“The Practice of Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted from above. But he did not stop there. Advancing further, he translated his words into actions, creating a direct example in the form of his own literature, marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus we get a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part set was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that we are extremely happy to present to the readers now Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

points.title: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as importan
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the au
summary: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of ling
points.body: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of linguistics and philology which touched also on history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books. Apart from the books mentioned above, some stories are from a volume of the authorʼs childrenʼs literature series – namely, In the Land of Hat́t́amálá.

points.body: Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs discourses, as published, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise wording the author used in speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words. As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. ‘Man is mortal’ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

points.body: Every new translation is reviewed by a “first editor” who compares the English translation with the original Bengali or Hindi. points.body: The people of Ráŕh [land of laterite soil; a territory mostly in West Bengal, stretching from the west bank of Bhagirathi River to the Parasnath Hills] engage in serious philosophical exercises as much as they engage in light-hearted play; they are full of life – with laughter, amusements, dance, song, wit and humour (rága and rauṋga). They are sociable and prefer to remain in each otherʼs company and in a cheerful mood (khos mejájii) in a gathering. Though burdened with poverty, they invite people for meals. They serve what they themselves eat – rice, black gram (biŕi in Ráŕhii Bengali), baŕi-posta [dumplings made of pulse, flavoured with poppy seeds], curry and pumpkin (d́iḿlá in Ráŕhii Bengali). They are not inhibited in their behaviour due to their poverty. They are not shy to say clearly what ought to be said. Here is an example of the straightforwardness of the people of Ráŕh: ( 1 )

points.body: It should be kept in mind that in linguistics, edicts are always correlated with interdicts. “Yes” and “No” are complementary to each other. One cannot exist without the other. This is true in every sphere. In philology, we therefore have to keep in mind that even if we forget the primary edicts, the exceptions (apaváda in Hindi) are to be remembered as much as possible.

points.body: For example, in English, if there is a single vowel before a single consonant, then when an inflection is added to the consonant, it is doubled. “Fit” in that case becomes “fitting”, “fitted”, etc. But there are exceptions as well – like “benefit” where, even with the addition of an inflection, the “t” is not doubled.

points.body: Speaking of epilepsy, I recall an incident. Once, a habitual addict of Krishnanagar had drunk to his gills and spent the night lying in a drain. A gentle breeze at the break of dawn and the touch of cold water flowing down the drain brought him to his senses. He opened his eyes and found a crowd looking down at him. He felt just a shade bashful and closed his eyes. [[He]] looked up again after a few moments. He discovered his sonʼs father-in-law (vaeváhika) gazing at him from the crowd which made him feel very ashamed.

points.body: The mother explained, “A woman who does not have a son has just one regret. She goes around lamenting that she is childless. A woman whose son has died also has just one regret. She beats her head in sorrow and cries, 'Oh, my son is gone forever, no one will call me má anymore!ʼ But a mother whose son is a fool is doomed forever. On the one hand, she is in misery all the time and on the other, her neighbours call upon her day in and day out to complain about the foolish deeds committed by the son. Listening and listening to all these noises day in and day out I am extremely vexed; my heart is keen to flee. Hence learned men have said, it is better not to have a son at all or even lose a son to death, rather than be saddled with a fool of a son all your life. If such is the case, a mother has to endure agony every moment. You can very well see the plight I am in with this fool Dantavikásh [literal meaning is to display oneʼs teeth foolishly]. Even the fox in the wild and mosquitoes in watery bogs cry in sympathy. Just see with your own eyes how cruelly he beat me on my back. It is swollen like a guŕ-pit́he.”

points.body: Shráddhe ca bhuribhojanam was a custom in the past. This meant that the invitees to a shráddha [a feast held after funeral rites are performed] were to be treated in a grand fashion. In its common usage, the meaning of the word bhuri is “plenty”, and in this context the quantity of luci, sweets, etc. that was packed inside the guestʼs stomach was to be served on an adjacent plate in an equal amount. After the meal was over, the other plateful of food was tied up in a bundle (cháṋdá) and taken home by the guest. Even after a surfeit of food (such a huge meal had been taken that the food had risen past the abdomen and chest and reached the throat), it was only when the guest carried an equal amount home that it was accepted that it had indeed been a grand feast (bhuribhojana).

points.body: “You tried your best again but to no avail,” said the priest. “The case for Shiva is the same. He might wear a tiger skin in the cremation ground, but do you expect him to come and move around in this locality wearing nothing or just a tiger skin! If he ever comes here, he will be wearing the finest dhoti and frilled páiṋjábii [upper dress] or pants and a bush shirt. However, making pants is troublesome because you need correct measurements and a good tailor. Why go to so much trouble? It is better to offer him a few fine quality dhotis from Pharasdanga or Shantipur. Many hundreds rupee notes are already in your hands by selling potatoes this year. Also, you can get these here by the dozen if you are willing to shell out money. Shiva is very easy to please. He is satisfied with whatever you offer to Him. He will not be unhappy if you give him dhotis made of coarse cloth, but I could not allow that! How can I ask him to wear cheap cloth? I have not lost my senses, have I? The other night, the Mother Goddess came in my dream. She said, 'I know that you work very hard in your profession. You walk miles in the sun and rain to reach the house of your devotees. I know that you were harassed (nástánábud ( 2 ) ) to the extreme on your way to Chandannagore the other day. My heart bled in sorrow for your sake. Tell your devotee to donate to you a cycle of the latest design and a good quality umbrella this time. You are my son. Tell him that I shall be pleased if he gives you a cycle and an umbrella.ʼ She further added, 'Tell your disciple that both are available in the central market in Chandannagore. He does not have to travel all the way to Kolkata to buy, and since he will be going to the central market, let him also buy five seers of sweet (gajá) [a type of sweet made of flour] to be given away as offering. It will look nice.”

points.body: Thakkarputra > t́hakkurputta > t́hakkarpua > t́hákurpo. Etymologically, t́hákurpo means the son of a womanʼs father-in-law. However, t́hákurpo, in common usage, is a form of addressing her deor [husbandʼs younger brother]. The reverse relationship or form of address is bháj or, in modern Bengali, baudi. points.body: He continued, “Potato is a major crop in Dhanekhali area. We did not keep sheep as pets because they dig up and eat the potatoes in the field. There were a number of ponds in our village with young, good quality fish, especially of the rui, kátlá and mrgel (mirik in western Ráŕh) variety. Rudd fish (kálibáus in western Ráŕh) was particularly good. The best district in Ráŕh is Hooghly, of which the best village is Takipur where our pond surrounded by palm trees is the best. Some rui fish in it are huge – as large as twenty buffaloes put together. They are so big... oh, how shall I show you the size! This is the problem... they were truly large... very large... as large as...” So saying, he extended his hands sideways and scooped up some water. “Sooo big... and do you know how wide they are?” As he said that he revolved his hands in a half-circle and sprinkled the water on his bald pate. He said, “So wide ... so wide ...” Finally, he brought his arms near his head and slapped it with the open palms and said, “Have you now got a measure of how wide they were?” Thus he repeated the description of the fishʼs size a few times, collecting water each time while explaining the length and soaked his head thoroughly while he gestured to show its width.

points.body: Ekanoŕe said, “You are a very good boy, and thatʼs why you feel pain on seeing the suffering of others. But not everyone is like that. Take my case, for example. I have studied a lot, taught in a college and a school of Sanskrit, and practised a little ayurvedic medicine. In those days I used to manufacture medicine of world-wide repute in my ayurvedic laboratory. There I made 'palatial-house powderʼ (brhat att́áliká curńa) and ‘giant elephant and gold compounded tablets’ (svarńaghatita subrhat hastii bhasma vatiká), and thousands upon thousands of them were sold each month. Now, you see, when success goes to oneʼs head, one loses compassion for oneʼs fellow men. That, indeed, happened to me. I took to adulterating my products. And then, in course of time, I lost everything. Today I am penniless, destitute, the scum of the earth. Dear prince, I have committed many sins and, as a result, have become Ekánoŕe ghost, and have had to set up house in the palm tree. Until these sins are neutralized by virtuous deeds, I wonʼt have peace of mind. Even now I think, twenty-four hours a day I think, in what way I may atone for these sins. Whenever I get the opportunity I try my best to do good to others. Always keep in mind, prince, that a bad deed will never have good results, and a good deed will never have bad results.”

points.body: Ekanoŕe said, “Yes, condensed milk. I really mean it. Other cows give milk when they are milked, but she used to give condensed milk sometimes freshly clotted, sometimes steaming, sometimes hot. You canʼt imagine how tasty and palatable it was. I can clearly remember, prince, that we once had such a severely cold winter that everything was quickly frozen, and even the waters of the river Ganges turned into ice. I wanted to take the launch from Chinsurah fish market to Naihati [24 Parganas District]. However, the launch service had stopped. After all, you canʼt expect a launch to travel over ice. As I wasnʼt one to be easily deterred, I drove over the ice of the Ganges on a motorcycle and in just one minute reached Naihati. There was no need to drive over the ice to get to Howrah from Calcutta as thereʼs a bridge. But a number of times I amused myself by driving up as far as Salkia Bandhaghat [in Howrah District] from Ahiritola [in Kolkata]. Oh, what a thrilling experience. Just thinking about it makes me jump with joy. Oh yes, let me return to what I was talking about. For some days during that very winter I milked the cow. On milking her I was astonished: 'My goodness, what happened to the condensed milk?ʼ It had turned to ice-cream. After that, for fifteen days at a stretch ice-cream came out of the cowʼs udder. That season I sold ice-cream and pocketed 500,000 rupees.”

points.body: We got the word cávi from Portuguese language. In Portuguese, cha is pronounced somewhat like sha. I heard both the Portuguese and Spanish people pronounce cávi shábi. Currently this word cávi is widely used both in Bengal and in the whole of North India. Surprisingly, even 450 years ago no one in this country was familiar with this word. In North India cávi used to be called kuiṋjii and in Bengal kát́hi. Even today some people in Ráŕh call tálá-cavi [ lock and key] kulup-kát́hi.
